https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/05/duna.text: Menü Kereső Aerial footage shows just how low Danube levels have dropped in and around Budapest English The Danube river at Szentendre – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Németh Sz. Péter Madzin Emília Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom The soutnern tip of Margit island with the Margit bridge – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The water level of the Danube river has never been as low in Budapest as it is now. Although the situation may improve minimally towards the end of the week and the prospects are more optimistic now than they were a few days ago, due to the extreme drought, the water level will likely continue to drop in the coming days. Because of the current heat wave, all sorts of interesting objects which had previously been submerged in the Danube have been emerging from the river that runs through the city: the remains of the former Franz Joseph Bridge are now visible beneath Szabadság Bridge; World War II explosive devices have been unearthed from the silt near Batthyány Square; and weapons have been recovered from the river near Margit Island. The aerial photos taken by photographer Ferenc Sztraka on July 30, along with his commentary provide an overview of what the Danube looks like these days between Budapest and Esztergom. All sorts of wild rumors have been circulating online about the causes behind the low water levels, but according to a statement from the National Water Authority, the primary cause of the extremely low water levels is typically the lack of precipitation in the watershed, which leads to low natural water yields. And while exploring the now-exposed Danube riverbed might be a tempting adventure, the Budapest Waterworks has strongly urged everyone not to venture into this area either for a sports activity or for other reasons, under any circumstances, as they are typically classified as water protection zones. “If, as a result of human activity (normally not present here), any pollution should occur in these currently accessible areas, the consequences could, in extreme cases, render that particular section of the water source unusable for years or even decades. In other words, that section could be excluded from the process of producing drinking water,” the Budapest Waterworks said. The northern tip of Margit island – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka “We flew north along Margit Island. I immediately noticed something interesting: when rivers are confined between levees, it is not easy to tell from the air whether the water level is high or low. Even when the river was flooding, the only clear indication was the strange angle at which the docks’ planks were tilted. “The situation was similar this time as well, except it was the other way around," wrote Sztraka. The southern tip of Óbudai Island and the entrance of the Újpest bay – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka In mid-July we reported on the Danube’s water flow being very low—just 835.6 cubic meters per second at the time—and, on top of that, the water’s temperature kept rising. Because of this, experts at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant returned to the continuous monitoring of the river's temperature along the affected section to ensure the safe operation of the plant and compliance with environmental regulations. By 2 August, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that the Danube’s water level is just one centimeter away from necessitating a complete shutdown of the power plant. As of Wednesday afternoon, this hasn’t happened yet; the last Paks turbine still in operation continues to generate power. The highest temperature previously recorded at the wter gauge on the Danube in Budapest was 27.2 degrees Celsius in August 2018; on the evening of June 30 this year, it already reached 28.2 degrees. This coincided with a heat wave peaking at 42 degrees, prompting Minister of Economy and Energy István Kapitány to authorize increasing the maximum temperature limit at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant from 30 to 31.5 degrees to ensure a secure power supply—a measure environmentalists said could only be maintained temporarily. A sandbar at the northern tip of Óbuda Island; the ongoing construction for the upcoming Sziget Festival is already visible – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka According to Sztraka, as they travelled further from the massive levee that characterizes the Budapest section of the river, the grim reality of the drought immediately became more pronounced. “At the northern tip of Óbuda Island, we were greeted by the sight of a sizable sandbar. It’s quite possible that those attending the Sziget Festival—the stages for which were under construction at the time—will immediately take possession of the sandy beach which will now come as a bonus with their ticket price. During the flight we noticed that a wide strip of sand now encircles each island all the way to Esztergom—and surely beyond as well. Népsziget and the almost dried out bay – Photo: Ference Sztraka The winter harbor in Újpest, also known as Népsziget Bay, is a 28.6-hectare bay in the capital. It is an important hub of Budapest’s water life and is a favorite destination for anglers and boaters alike. The Kossuth public beach on Római part – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The southern tip of Szentendrei Island and the Megyeri bridge – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Apart from the two anchored tankers visible near the southern tip of Szentendrei Island, the photographer did not see any bigger sightseeing or cargo ships along the entire route. Due to the extremely low water level, boat traffic has also come to a standstill. The Rév street Dunayacht quay in Megyer, and the remains of a ship visible in the water – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Even at the Dunayacht boating station on Rév Street in Megyer, the water is not deep enough to receive bigger vessels. More than a dozen hotel boats have been stranded along the Hungarian section of the Danube in recent days due to the low water levels, and most cargo ships have also been forced to stay put. The remains of what appears to be a ship have also emerged from the water near Megyer. The mouth of the Szilas Stream, located on the south side of the Megyeri Bridge – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The mouth of the Szilas Stream, located on the south side of the Megyeri Bridge has taken on a rather strange, tropical-like appearance, with what looks like several-previously not visible-tires scattered across the riverbed. Lupa island and the Megyeri bridge from the north – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Sediment formation in the river is also clearly visible near Lupa Island. A ferry at Szürkő island, between Horány and Dunakeszi – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The ferry was still running between Horány and Dunakeszi by Szürkő Island, although some of the boats on the island were already stranded on dry land. Protruding sandbars at Szentendre – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The Danube near Szentendre, with the Tildy bridge in Tahitótfalu – Photo Ferenc Sztraka “The Tildy Bridge in Tahitótfalu comes into view suddenly when flying over the Szentendre section of the Danube. Near the bridge, on the side of the island, the exposed sandbar is wider, but at the next bend in the river, the alluvial deposits that have surfaced turn up on the opposite side,” wrote Sztraka. The public beach in Dunabogdány – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The public beach in Dunabogdány was bustling with activity when the photos were taken. This is the settlement whose residents refused to reduce their water consumption despite repeated warnings—until the ice eventually broke and they began to exercise restraint, which even earned them special praise from the waterworks. The curve above Szentpéteri Island – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The harbour at Kisoroszi – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Things weren't looking too good at the Kisoroszi ferry crossing either. Kisoroszi, a village of nearly 1,000 residents located on Szentendre Island, is best known for becoming completely cut off from the outside world by floodwaters almost each time there is major flooding on the Danube. Two years ago, the water level was so high that the road connecting Kisoroszi and Tahitótfalu had to be closed. In recent days, however, 89 percent of the country has been experiencing a moderately severe or severe drought. Sólyom Island and riders on the sandbar – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka “Whenever I’m flying over the Danube Bend, I always look out for Sólyom Island, located at the northern tip of Szentendre Island. Even during a minor drop in water levels, a fairly large sandbar tends to form here quickly, but I’ve never seen this much exposed land in this spot before. There were beachgoers here too, and from high above, we spotted something moving quite fast. At first we got excited, thinking that there were zebras running around, but as we got closer, it turned out to be just two adult horses and a foal galloping below us.” The northern tip of Szentendre Island at Kisoroszi – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The Visegrád Citadel, with the tip of the Szentendre island at Kisoroszi in the background – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The view from the Visegrád Citadel is truly dramatic. From here, you can see all the way to the tip of Kisoroszi Island. No wonder the town is one of the most popular tourist destinations in the country. A strangely shaped formation under the water along the Upper Bay in Visegrád – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Sandbars at the estuary of Ipoly – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The sandbar in front of Sas Hill – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka “The sandbar located in front of Sas Hill, halfway between Pilismarót and Esztergom, at the foot of the infamous Hideglelős Cross, becomes visible even during minor droughts, though not nearly as much as now. This part of the landscape is one of my personal favorites.” The Kis-Duna in Esztergom – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka There isn’t much water left in the Little Danube (Kis-Duna) in Esztergom either; the photos clearly show that due to the current water level, the motorboats are neatly parked one behind the other. The Prímás Island just above Esztergom – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Once we reached the westernmost point of our journey at Prímás Island above Esztergom, we turned around to head home. A small trickle of fresh water could still be seen flowing towards the upper part of the island here. As a side note, I would like to mention that when I first saw the Danube from an airplane in February 1990, in very gray weather, it was anything but blue. But under the right weather conditions—against the backdrop of a blue sky on clear days—the Danube truly does appear blue, just like every other river and lake in Hungary that I’ve flown over”, Sztraka writes in conclusion. Körtvélyes Island between Esztergom and Tát – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The situation isn’t only dramatic in Hungary. All of Europe is suffering from the heat. Power plants, factories, and industrial facilities are shutting down or reducing production one after another. Water levels have dropped to dangerously low in several rivers, leading to restrictions or even the suspension of navigation, which is causing billions of euros in damage to the continent’s economy. We still have some tough days ahead of us though. According to Időkép’s forecast, daytime highs will hover around 40 degrees Celsius in Hungary through Thursday, but midweek temperatures could reach as high as 42 degrees, which would set a new record for the second time this summer. Occasional thunderstorms may develop, and at night, temperatures will only drop to between 20–25 degrees Celsius.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c998.text: Image source, Reuters By David Gritten Published 5 hours ago One person has been killed in an Israeli strike in southern Lebanon, the country's health ministry says, after the Israeli military said it was responding to a "blatant violation of the ceasefire" by the Iran-backed group Hezbollah. A man died and 12 other people were injured when the roof of a prayer hall at the cemetery of the town of Tibnin was hit, according to Lebanese media. Strikes were also reported to the west in the town of Mansouri, where the Israeli military issued its first evacuation order for more than a month. Hezbollah has not commented on the events, which came as Israeli and Lebanese officials attended US-sponsored talks in Rome aimed at maintaining the ceasefire. In late June, the three countries agreed a trilateral framework that should see the Israeli military gradually withdraw from territory it is occupying in southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah. Two weeks ago, the Lebanese army was allowed to deploy to one of the first "pilot zones", after Israeli troops pulled out of the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Hezbollah has rejected the agreement, saying the provisions linking Israel's withdrawal to the group's disarmament crossed "all red lines". The Israeli military announced that it had begun carrying out "precise strikes" in southern Lebanon on Wednesday afternoon, about 30 minutes after its Arabic spokesperson had told residents of Mansouri to evacuate ahead of "forceful action" there. Both statements accused Hezbollah of violating the ceasefire but gave no further details. However, an Israeli military source told Israeli media that displaced residents of Mansouri had returned to their town "under the auspices of the Lebanese army, which established a checkpoint in the area in violation of the agreements". The source said the town was inside the Israeli-declared "security zone" - a 10km (six-mile) deep strip of occupied Lebanese territory running along the border - and "military activity that endangers the lives of Lebanese civilians" was taking place there. The evacuation order was the first issued in southern Lebanon since 14 June, when residents of 29 towns and villages were told to flee their homes. Earlier on Wednesday, the mayor of Mansouri, Haidar Madihli, told local media that Israeli warplanes had carried out four strikes on buildings and villas in the Ghazaleh neighbourhood on the outskirts of the town, causing extensive damage to the targeted structures. The strikes triggered a wave of displacement, with families filling cars with their belongings and heading towards Tyre, the largest city in the south, Madihli said. He added that around 120 families had returned to Mansouri after the 19 June ceasefire, but that the number had steadily fallen as Israeli strikes intensified. In recent days, only 40 to 50 families remained in the town. The evacuation order came as the UN's humanitarian office said more than 820,000 people displaced in Lebanon by the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah had begun returning to their home areas following a reduction in hostilities. However, the UN said about 360,000 other people remained displaced across Lebanon, including 26,000 living in government shelters. Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader. Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. At least 4,333 people have been killed during the conflict, including 392 women and 253 children, according to the Lebanese health ministry. Since the ceasefire was announced, the ministry has recorded the killing of 353 people. Israeli authorities say 38 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed on both sides of the border during the conflict. Gray-Zone Warfare Picks Easy Targets in Germany Political appeasement won’t buy off hostile powers. An aircraft colliding with a mysterious object near the same airport. Interference in upcoming state elections. Foreign agents scoping out a little-known defense CEO. Germany has been the target of a wide range of mysterious activities over the last couple of months—the type that analysts usually label as “gray-zone” (my preferred term) or “hybrid” warfare. Hybrid threats, in Frank Hoffmann’s classic definition , “incorporate a full range of different modes of warfare including conventional capabilities, irregular tactics and formations, terrorist acts including indiscriminate violence and coercion, and criminal disorder.” A sophisticated drone discovered inside a German airport. An aircraft colliding with a mysterious object near the same airport. Interference in upcoming state elections. Foreign agents scoping out a little-known defense CEO. Germany has been the target of a wide range of mysterious activities over the last couple of months—the type that analysts usually label as “gray-zone” (my preferred term) or “hybrid” warfare. Hybrid threats, in Frank Hoffmann’s classic definition , “incorporate a full range of different modes of warfare including conventional capabilities, irregular tactics and formations, terrorist acts including indiscriminate violence and coercion, and criminal disorder.” Gray-zone acts, by contrast, involve no conventional military element; to use military-wonk parlance, they’re not kinetic. In the recent string of such acts in Germany, the very likely culprit is Russia, which has a history of using these techniques against European states. European governments have linked the Kremlin to, among other things, a massive shopping mall fire in Warsaw, an attack on property linked to then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer, and facilitating migrants arriving at the borders of Norway and Finland. But targeting Germany has particular significance: It shows that, when it comes to targets for gray-zone warfare, the stance of a state matters far less than its vulnerability. Germany has spent decades calling for peace and cooperation, but those earnest sentiments have not prevented it becoming a target. What does this look like on the ground? Some of it is perplexing scenarios like the mysterious drone spotted at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany hovering near aircraft belonging to Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines. The drone was equipped with anti-detection technology, but made a clumsy landing, Die Zeit reported , and had accidentally dropped its load of 600 grams of semtex, a high-grade explosive, on the ground nearby. Leipzig/Halle, it’s worth remembering, is not just the region’s leading airport; it’s also a crucial hub for military supplies bound for Ukraine. The authorities have not yet identified those involved in the drone incident, but the investigative trail will almost certainly lead to Russia. In Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, meanwhile, election campaigns are in full swing for the two states’ parliamentary elections this September. In Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is polling above 40 percent , and in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it’s by far the largest party, hovering around 36 percent . The AfD is not only far right but also more sympathetic to Russia than other German parties. An online campaign, almost certainly sponsored by Russia, thus flooded the internet with fake content discrediting other parties’ candidates. The sophisticated campaign features posts that look like they come from legitimate accounts like mainstream news organizations. It also does some personal targeting, including the campaign directed against Stefan Thumann, the CEO of a mid-sized German firm called Donaustahl that supplies drones to Ukriane. Because Donaustahl is not a high-profile company, Thumann may have assumed this was just another business deal. Not so. This month, German authorities, acting on a tip from a foreign ally, arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman who had been tracking his daily life, including visiting his home. The German prosecution has accused them of acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence agency. All this is business as usual for Russia, which has employed similar tools for decades. But what makes this spate noteworthy is that it’s directed at Germany, a country that promotes cooperation and understanding like no other. For German politicians over the past decades, there has been no conflict that could not be tackled through negotiations, no dispute too thorny for multilateral negotiations. It co-founded what is now the European Union. It was a key participant in the Iran nuclear deal negotiations. It tried to solve Russia’s 2014 attacks on Ukraine through diplomatic talks . When the country itself reunited in 1990, it did so after orderly negotiations with World War II’s four victors. For the most part, this constructive approach worked. Why would anyone want to harm such a sensible and collaborative nation? Because they can. After more than a decade of mapping gray-zone actions, I have concluded that gray-zone aggressors are actors of convenience. They don’t target countries, sectors, or groups because they’re particularly high-profile or combative: They target them because they are low-hanging fruit. Earlier this year, Russian hackers stole images from CCTV and door cameras across Europe—and then published them to mock Western authorities. For many months now, Russian transmitters have been jamming and spoofing GPS signals in the Baltic Sea region, making it much harder for ships and aircraft to navigate. Russia is not the world’s only perpetrator of gray-zone aggression. Earlier this summer, residents of small towns across Minnesota were shocked to find that their water plants had been attacked by cyber teams thought to be linked to Iran. Minnesota is a blue state locked in a contentious battle with the Trump administration, but the alleged Iranian actors apparently cared less about political positions than relatively easy targets. In fact, perpetrators of gray-zone activities can keep testing targets. Some attacks will succeed, some won’t, and if an attack fails, no matter: Since Western countries don’t retaliate eye for eye—or at all—the attacker’s cost-benefit calculus is extremely advantageous. (This is precisely why I called my book on gray-zone aggression The Defender’s Dilemma .) That has led to the paradoxical reality that Germany, which used to be highly moderate in its criticism of Russia, is as likely to be the target of gray-zone activity as Estonia, which has for years loudly warned of Russian threats. To be sure, Germany these days is as forceful in its criticism of Russia as Estonia is—but it apparently gets no credit for decades of cooperative efforts. Politicians might hope to avoid making their countries targets of gray-zone attacks, but keeping a low profile doesn’t seem to work. And whatever the country may be, keeping the public informed is indispensable. At Leipzig/Halle Airport, an eagle-eyed airport worker first spotted the drone in the middle of the night. Being nice is good. Staying alert is better. https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/drone-crashe.text: Europe Drone crashes in Romania after entering airspace near Ukrainian border Incident occurs amid ongoing Russian military activity in neighboring Ukraine Diyar Güldoğan 20 August 2026 • Update : 20 August 2026 WASHINGTON DC A drone entered Romanian airspace early Thursday and crashed in an unpopulated area of Tulcea County, Romania’s Defense Ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that its radar system detected a group of aerial targets near the Ukrainian border at 2.23 a.m. local time (2323GMT Wednesday). Two Spanish Air and Space Force F-18 fighter jets were scrambled to monitor the situation, while a Romanian Air Force IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter conducted an aerial reconnaissance mission. At 3:21 a.m. (0021GMT), a drone entered Romanian airspace about 13 kilometers (8 miles) east of Galati. Three minutes later, the Romanian helicopter crew reported that the drone had crashed approximately 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) northeast of Grindu village in Tulcea County in an uninhabited area. The impact triggered a fire, which extinguished itself, according to the ministry. No casualties or material damage were reported. A military team was sent to the crash site to secure the area and examine the wreckage. https://thebulletin.org/2026/08/the-us-m.text: About Magazine Events Contact Store My Account Login Donate Give Now Ways To Give What Your Gift Supports Annual Event Einstein Circle Legacy Society Donor-Advised Fund The US military’s fatal stance on climate change The Pentagon is preparing to wage war in a warmer world, even as it accelerates it An Oregon Army National Guard HH-60M Black Hawk crew with Golf Company, 1st Battalion, 189th Aviation, flew water bucket missions on the Hagen Fire in Umatilla County, Oregon, Aug. 10, 2026. (Oregon National Guard photo by Maj. W. Chris Clyne) Share Copy link Linked copied Email Facebook Bluesky Twitter LinkedIn WhatsApp Reddit Spread By Neta C. Crawford August 27, 2026 The US military has a long, complicated relationship with climate change. Beginning in the mid-1950s, it paid for research into greenhouse gases and the many ways global warming could make operations more difficult and less predictable. As early as the 1990s, the Navy began raising piers to protect its ports and working to make its facilities more resilient to frequent flooding. In 2007, Sherri Goodman, the Pentagon’s first Chief Environmental Officer, coined the phrase “threat multiplier” to convey the idea that climate change could exacerbate geopolitical instability and other security risks. All branches of the military are currently preparing for more humanitarian rescue relief work as environmental emergencies multiply. But even while it’s adapting for this hot new world, with its emergencies and imminent threats, the military has largely sidestepped its role in creating the climate crisis. For decades, the military has been a significant contributor to global warming, but there is no full accounting of military and war-related emissions . Military industrial emissions are also high, and the global volume and value of arms transfers has grown rapidly over the past half-decade. And then of course, by destroying infrastructure and the environment, war itself contributes to global warming. The argument that climate change is a threat multiplier short circuits the causal chain: War and military buildups are climate change multipliers. And, while it is true that the climate is warming at an accelerating rate and that the window for preventing the worst outcomes is closing, the national security establishment’s impulse—to focus on national security threats that may or may not be caused by climate change—may make us less secure because it increases military emissions and siphons resources from emissions reduction, the energy transition, and adaptation. “More serious than most people tend to believe” In November 1959, Edward Teller , the father of the hydrogen bomb, told petroleum executives that the world would soon need other sources of energy because fossil fuels were “contaminating the atmosphere.” It has been calculated that a temperature rise corresponding to a 10 per cent increase in carbon dioxide will be sufficient to melt the icecap and submerge New York. All the coastal cities would be covered, and since a considerable percentage of the human race lives in coastal regions, I think that this chemical contamination is more serious than most people tend to believe. In testimony before the House Committee on Appropriations in 1956, Roger Revelle—the noted climate change scientist and former naval officer—recommended researching how carbon dioxide emissions could “cause a remarkable change in the climate.” But even then, the priority was on military security and great power competition. As warming continued, Revelle said: the Arctic Ocean will become navigable and … then the Russian Arctic coastline will be really quite free for shipping…. This would have the effect, if it does happen, of changing the character of the Russians opposed to ourselves. We are now the greatest maritime nation on the earth. … If the Russian coastline increases by something like 2,000 miles or so, the Russians will become a great maritime nation. Yamal, a Russian nuclear-powered icebreaker, taking tourists to the North Pole in 2001. (Wofratz/Wikipedia) While many were debating in the 1990s whether climate change was a “hoax,” the military was considering the implications of global warming for their operations. Military forces depend on a functioning ecosystem. A 1990 Naval War College study by Terry P. Kelley described “significant effects” of global warming for the military, including how changes in the salinity, chemistry, and temperature of water would affect acoustic characteristics of oceans, impacting sonar performance. Indeed, the Navy was already conducting research on how the speed of sound in water increases as the temperature rises. Kelley also described how high winds, greater turbulence, and changes in ocean currents and the shape and underwater character of coastlines would affect operations. Sea level rise would expand the reach of shallow water and potentially “extend some target beaches 100 km inland,” potentially requiring alterations to amphibious assault equipment and tactics. Arguing that the effects of climate change would be greatest for the Navy, Kelley recommended that the Navy develop a long-term plan to reduce its infrastructure and facilities and redesign its bases and ships to deal with likely challenges. Like Revelle, Kelley foresaw potential opportunities for navigation with Arctic ice melting, but he also noted the potential for boundary tensions to become “severe” in areas where climate change caused drought and flooding and stressed the ability of people to have fresh water or grow food. Although the Office of Naval Research funded much of the early climate change research, the Defense Department successfully pushed to omit most reporting of military emissions from global climate agreements like the Kyoto Protocol. The Defense Department knew it was the United States’ largest petroleum user and said so. It also knew that its emissions would come under scrutiny if they were known, and that pursuing preeminence was emissions-intensive and undermined global climate goals. Marines drag a tree branch during a base cleanup effort following Hurricane Lala at Marine Corps Base Hawaii, Aug. 17, 2026. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Nicholas Figueroa) Climate change as threat multiplier? Not so fast While environmental stress can increase tension, academic analyses have not shown a strong or direct causal link between climate change and armed conflict. Nevertheless, the threat multiplier frame remains dominant and essentially unquestioned. In 2021, the Department of Homeland Security argued that climate change was “reshaping the risk landscape” and predicted a “global increase in natural disasters will … drive up the number and severity of humanitarian crises” with what it called “sweeping implications for regional and border security and core national security interests.” More ominously, the department also predicted that “revisionist nations will seek to exploit climate change induced instability to erode the rules-based order that is central to the security and prosperity of the United States and its allies.” NATO and the UN Security Council have also adopted the framing of climate change as a threat multiplier. In his introduction to the 2024 “ Department of Defense Climate Adaptation Plan, 2024-27 ,” Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin wrote that climate change posed strategic risks: Climate change fundamentally alters the conditions that shape military operations at home and around the world. At the same time, climate change is reshaping our strategic interests. As changes in the physical environment create the opportunity for well-prepared forces to secure a competitive advantage, deter aggression, and protect the United States and its interests, the Department of Defense (DOD) must both understand and adapt to the ways in which extreme weather and climate change affect our readiness and capabilities. In the same report, the Defense Department, asserted as fact its assumption that climate change “continues to increase the demand … for military operations at home and around the world.” The frame is how “missions and operations are adversely impacted by climate change through amplifying operational demands on the force, degrading installations, infrastructure, and systems, and increasing health risks to Service members.” The focus is on adaptation and technical fixes. The US national security establishment prioritizes the short term over all else: the operational challenges caused by climate change, the expenses of adaptation and repair, the race for resources, and the potential that climate change will cause war. As the United States 2021 National Intelligence Estimate said, “The current pace of transition to low- or zero-emission clean energy sources is not fast enough to avoid temperatures rising above the Paris goal of 1.5˚C.” That report predicted increasingly serious consequences for human security and increased risks to US national security. And it bolded their conclusion that, “ The increasing physical effects of climate change are likely to exacerbate cross-border geopolitical flashpoints as states take steps to secure their interests. ” Echoing the predictions of the 1950s and 1990s, the report asserts that the melting of sea ice in the Arctic will amplify “strategic competition” over resources in the region. Elsewhere, as temperatures rise and more extreme effects manifest, there is a growing risk of conflict over water and migration, particularly after 2030, and an increasing chance that countries will unilaterally test and deploy large-scale solar geoengineering—creating a new area of geopolitical disputes. The US national security community’s approach to climate has not only been mirrored by NATO but amplified by private organizations such as the International Military Council on Climate Security, which produces an annual World Climate and Security Report . These doomsday scenarios often ignore the necessity of emissions reductions and capacity building. They are lifeboat and drawbridge approaches to security on the assumption that it is already too late. The figures below, from the 2022 Department of Defense Climate Risk Analysis , illustrates the assessment that climate change will lead to conflict and increased demand for the military to perform humanitarian missions. ​ Defense Department views of climate change. Top: Examples of connections between climate hazards, primary and secondary climate impacts, and security implications. Bottom: Selected regional hazards worsened by climate change (key to symbols on the top row above map) and identified security implications (key to symbols on the bottom row below the map). This map illustrates some of the key risks by region, but is not comprehensive of all risk. (2022 Department of Defense Climate Risk Analysis) But none of these potential future paths to instability and conflict are a necessary consequence of climate change. Many of the potential causes of instability are unlikely or can be avoided . Negotiations, diplomacy, adaptation, and emissions reductions can all help to reduce the likelihood of these nightmare scenarios. The national security establishment recognizes the short-term impacts of climate change—the operational challenges, the expenses of adaptation and repair, the race for resources, and the possibility it will cause increased tension and war. This strategic and military policy response to climate change is practical in some tactical respects, but it is shortsighted and potentially counterproductive because it does not attend to Earth systems or the role of the military, military industry, and war as significant contributors to climate change . Ripple effects While adaptation is prudent, an ounce of prevention in the form of military and military industrial emissions reduction is essential to the cure. Justifying more military spending because climate change might cause insecurity is potentially counterproductive. Although the United States is not directly causally responsible for the military and military industrial emissions of every other country, because it is so militarily powerful, it does have a large share of responsibility for the strategies and procurement other countries, as they respond to US actions by increasing their own spending. For decades, the United States has advocated for increasing the military spending and procurement of NATO countries. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute documented a 41 percent increase in global military spending from 2016 through 2025; Germany’s military spending alone grew 118 percent between 2016 and 2025. Of course, since 2022, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has also been an important driver of NATO military mobilization. Soldiers provide security during Dragon 24, a NATO training event, at Bemowo Piskie Training Area, Poland, in March 2024. The exercise highlights NATO’s allied military cooperation and movement capabilities. (U.S. Army photo by Spc. Brett Thompson) Similarly, the dynamic of action-and-reaction in the Asia-Pacific region has driven up not only military spending but likely also military emissions. China’s military spending and military modernization have significantly increased in recent years— 62 percent between 2016 and 2025 according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. US allies in the Indo-Pacific region are both dependent on US forces and responsive to calls for more arms and mobilization to deter China. Canada has committed to purchasing 12 submarines that are capable of being deployed to defend Taiwan. Taiwan’s military spending has increased 59 percent during this same period. To the extent that the United States and its allies appear threatening, US doctrine, presence, and modernization plans also drive the emissions of its potential adversaries, including China. Several NATO countries have said they will reduce military emissions. But even emissions reductions from increased energy efficiency and the transition to renewable energy may be offset by military mobilization. For instance, Stuart Parkinson tracked 20 NATO member’s plans for emissions reduction. He found that even countries that reduced their military emissions a great deal, Germany and UK, had achieved a good portion of those reductions because the entire country had decarbonized its national grid. As military spending and mobilization grow, research shows that a state’s overall energy consumption tends to increase as military mobilization and military industrialization shape the economies of states toward high emission activities and technologies. Several academic and think tank analyses show that increased military spending—which is associated with more operations, more war, and more purchases of military equipment— increases military and military-industrial emissions . Because this sector is so reliant on fossil fuels, rising military spending jeopardizes climate targets. More recently, military spending has boosted greenhouse gas emissions in the civilian sector by its demand for artificial intelligence and quantum computing, an energy hungry sector of the economy. Like the internet , AI has been both paid for and then used by the US military . The Defense Department announced in May 2026 that its AI use had increased 1,775 percent over the past calendar year. The Defense Department, which says that it will be an “AI-first” fighting force, has forged agreements with SpaceX, OpenAI, Google, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, and Reflection to use their capabilities for warfighting and other applications. But this military funding for AI has also shaped the research and the demand for artificial intelligence in the larger economy, boosting AI energy use overall. https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/lithuan.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.10.09 10:02 Lithuania earmarks EUR 4.8bn for defence in 2027 budget Translated by Karolis Broga Source: ELTA Mindaugas Sinkevičius PHOTO: Žygimantas Gedvila | Elta Follow Delfi on Google The Lithuanian Government plans to allocate 5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), or EUR 4.8 billion, to defence in next year’s budget. It also intends to earmark EUR 150 million for measures under the Family Package aimed at addressing demographic challenges. Compared with this year’s National Defence Ministry budget, funding is expected to increase by EUR 36 million next year. „This is an important commitment to continue what has been started – […] the actual amount will still increase compared with this year’s allocation. The percentage will decrease, but the actual amount allocated to defence and security will rise,“ Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told reporters at the Government headquarters on Thursday. This year’s National Defence Ministry budget totals EUR 4.79 billion, or 5.38 percent of GDP. According to the prime minister, nearly 44 percent of the total allocation has been spent so far. Under the Government’s previously announced Family Package, next year’s allocations will include EUR 61.35 million for childcare and employment guarantees, EUR 40 million for housing support, EUR 25 million for increased pension entitlements linked to raising children, EUR 18 million for a support package for primary school pupils and EUR 5.65 million for increased sickness benefits. The budget projections presented by the prime minister also include EUR 980 million to support socially vulnerable people, EUR 115 million to index social benefits and EUR 172 million in additional health insurance contributions. A further EUR 450 million is earmarked for wage increases next year. The average old-age pension is expected to rise by around 10.4 percent, or EUR 78, to EUR 825 next year. For pensioners with the required contribution record, the average pension will rise by around 10.9 percent, or EUR 88, to EUR 895. The Government plans to use 9.4 percent of the State Social Insurance Fund (Sodra) budget surplus to index pensions. In total, an additional EUR 715.5 million will be needed in the 2027 budget to increase pensions. According to the prime minister, the budget projections will be presented at a meeting of the coalition council on Thursday, while the draft budget is expected to be formally submitted on Friday. Once the Government approves the draft budget prepared by the Finance Ministry, it will be sent to the Seimas for consideration. https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text: Archaeologists found the personal belongings in a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, once one of Pompeii’s busiest streets. Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological Park View image in fullscreen Archaeologists found the personal belongings in a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, once one of Pompeii’s busiest streets. Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological Park Archaeology Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79 Angela Giuffrida in Rome Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.06 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 12.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii. The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii. The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern. View image in fullscreen A charm from a crepundia, a type of necklace often worn by children. Photograph: via Pompeii Archaeological Park But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury. The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified. “A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park. “It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.” The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson. The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said. Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home. View image in fullscreen Bronze weights and a box closure found among the possessions. Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological Park The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its ​facade was first excavated ​in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project. There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century. View image in fullscreen A bronze oil lamp with a deflector. Photograph: SV_POMPEII/via Pompeii Archaeological Park “It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters. “So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.” Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city. A home containing a cramped bakery , where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.
